extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Huitzilopochtli's birth is a pivotal myth. Coatlicue, while sweeping a temple, was impregnated by a feather and miraculously conceived Huitzilopochtli. Her other children, Coyolxauhqui (goddess of the moon) and the Centzon Huitznahua (the four hundred stars), saw this as an insult and plotted to kill her. However, Huitzilopochtli sprang forth fully armed, slaying Coyolxauhqui and scattering the Centzon Huitznahua. This event symbolizes the daily victory of the sun over the moon and stars. His guidance of the Mexica from Aztlan to the Valley of Mexico is another central myth. He communicated his will through priests and dreams, leading them to the promised land where they would build their magnificent city.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Huitzilopochtli was the patron deity of the Mexica people and the city of Tenochtitlan. His worship was central to Aztec state religion and ideology. He represented the divine mandate for Aztec expansion and military conquest. Human sacrifice, particularly of war captives, was seen as essential to sustain him and the sun, ensuring the continuation of life and cosmic order. The Templo Mayor, the main temple in Tenochtitlan, was dedicated to him and Tlaloc (god of rain), highlighting his importance. His priests held significant political power, interpreting his will and directing state affairs. He was a powerful symbol of Aztec identity, power, and destiny.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Huitzilopochtli embodies several layers of symbolism. As the "Hummingbird of the South," he represents the vibrant energy of the sun and the warrior spirit. The hummingbird itself is associated with war and vitality. His role as a solar deity links him to themes of light, life, and victory over darkness. The act of human sacrifice, while brutal, was interpreted as a sacred exchange: offering the most precious thing (human life) to sustain the sun and ensure the continuation of the world. He also represents the Mexica people's resilience, determination, and divine right to rule. The myth of his birth and victory over his siblings represents the triumph of order over chaos.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: While the Aztec empire was destroyed by the Spanish conquest, Huitzilopochtli remains a significant figure in understanding Aztec culture and religion. He is a symbol of pre-Columbian Mexico and a reminder of the complex religious and cosmological beliefs of the Aztec civilization. In modern Mexico, he is sometimes invoked in cultural and artistic expressions, representing a connection to the indigenous past. His story continues to be studied by scholars and inspires artistic interpretations. He appears in books, movies, and other media that explore Aztec mythology. Though the practice of human sacrifice is condemned, the underlying themes of sacrifice, renewal, and the cyclical nature of life and death continue to resonate.

description: Huitzilopochtli, meaning "Hummingbird of the South" or "Left-Handed Hummingbird," was a central deity in the Aztec pantheon. He embodied war, the sun, and human sacrifice, playing a crucial role in Aztec cosmology and state ideology. According to legend, he was born fully armed from his mother Coatlicue after she was impregnated by a ball of feathers. Immediately after his birth, he defended her from his siblings who were angered by her supposed dishonor. Huitzilopochtli guided the Mexica people on their long migration, instructing them to settle where they found an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a serpent, which became the foundation of Tenochtitlan. He required constant nourishment through human sacrifice to sustain the sun's journey across the sky and ensure the continuation of the world. His worship was deeply intertwined with warfare and imperial expansion, justifying the Aztec's military campaigns as a means of acquiring sacrificial victims.
